A smear is something — a substance, a stain, or a damaging claim — that has been spread across something else, usually in a thin, messy, or deliberate way. The word almost always carries a sense of dirtiness, messiness, or harm, depending on the context.
Meaning 1: A dirty mark or stain on a surface

This is the most everyday meaning. When a soft, wet, or greasy substance gets rubbed across a surface and leaves a messy streak or blotch behind, that mark is called a smear.

The key quality of a smear (versus, say, a drop or a spot) is that it has been spread — it stretches across an area rather than sitting neatly in one place.

Examples:

  • There was a smear of grease on the car window.
  • The toddler left smears of chocolate all over the wall.
  • The detective noticed a smear of blood on the door handle.
  • Her glasses were covered in smears from fingerprints.

A smear tends to look messy and unintentional. It's the kind of mark you don't want to see on a clean surface.
Meaning 2: A thin layer of a soft substance (spread deliberately)

Here, the word is used more neutrally — without implying dirtiness. A smear can simply be a small amount of a soft substance that has been spread thinly over something. This meaning is common in cooking and everyday life.

Examples:

  • She put a thin smear of butter on her toast.
  • He applied a smear of ointment to the wound.
  • The recipe calls for just a smear of mustard on the bread.

Notice how in this sense, a smear is not a large or generous amount — it's specifically a thin, light coating. If someone gives you "a smear of peanut butter," it's barely enough. This distinguishes it from a "dollop" (a larger blob) or a "layer" (more even and substantial).
Meaning 3: A false or damaging statement meant to ruin someone's reputation

This is a very important and widely used meaning, especially in politics, journalism, and public life.

A smear in this sense is a false, misleading, or unfair accusation or story spread about a person in order to damage how others see them. The person spreading the smear usually wants to destroy the target's reputation, credibility, or career — often without any solid evidence.

The logic behind this usage connects to the physical meaning: just like a dirty smear leaves a stain on a clean surface that's hard to remove, a reputational smear leaves a "stain" on a person's name that can be hard to wash off, even if it's completely untrue.

Examples:

  • The newspaper article was a smear against the politician — none of the claims were verified.
  • He called the accusations a smear designed to stop his campaign.
  • She dismissed the story as a smear by her rivals.

A very common compound you will encounter is a smear campaign — this means an organized, deliberate effort (often by political opponents, rivals, or enemies) to spread a series of damaging, false, or exaggerated claims about someone over time. It's not just one accusation, but a sustained, coordinated effort to destroy a person's public image.

Example:

  • The opposition party launched a smear campaign against the candidate, spreading rumors about his past.

The word "smear" in this context is almost always negative — it implies the attack is unfair, dishonest, or based on lies. If someone calls something a "smear," they are signaling they believe the accusation is false and motivated by malice.
Meaning 4: A medical or scientific sample spread on a slide

In medicine and science, a smear refers to a sample of cells, tissue, blood, or other biological material that has been thinly spread onto a glass slide so it can be examined under a microscope.

Examples:

  • The doctor ordered a blood smear to check for infection.
  • A throat smear was taken to identify the bacteria causing her illness.

The most well-known example is the Pap smear (also called a cervical smear) — a routine medical test for women in which cells are gently scraped from the cervix and spread on a slide to check for early signs of cancer or other abnormalities. You will frequently hear this term in the context of women's health.

All four meanings connect back to one central idea: something spread across a surface or a space. Whether it's grease on a window, butter on bread, lies about a person, or cells on a glass slide — the common thread is always spreading.

Outside of the medical and food contexts (where the word is fairly neutral), smear tends to carry a negative or unpleasant feeling. A smear on glass is unwanted. A smear on a reputation is harmful. Even in casual use, calling something a smear implies messiness, carelessness, or bad intent.

This is a word you'll see often in political news ("smear campaign"), in everyday conversation ("wipe that smear off the mirror"), and in medical contexts ("Pap smear"). Now you're equipped for all of them.
